title: “ABOVE ALL, LOVE EACH OTHER DEEPLY” — WHY PETER CONNECTED LOVE WITH SIN
paragraphs: “ABOVE ALL, LOVE EACH OTHER DEEPLY” — WHY PETER CONNECTED LOVE WITH SIN
Peter knew what it was like to fail Jesus publicly. Maybe that is why, when he wrote about the sins that can tear believers apart, he did not begin with punishment. He began with love.
There is something almost unsettling about the way Peter says it.
Not because the words are difficult.
Because the man writing them knew exactly what it felt like to need them.
“Above all, keep loving one another earnestly, since love covers a multitude of sins.” — 1 Peter 4:8
Read that again slowly.
Above all.
Not when everybody behaves.
Not when nobody disappoints you.
Not when the church finally becomes filled with people who never misunderstand you, offend you, fail you, speak carelessly, forget you, frustrate you, or hurt you.
Peter writes to real Christians living in a real world filled with suffering, pressure, weakness, temptation, persecution, personality conflicts, wounds, and human failure.
And right there, he says:
Above all...
love.
But there is something even deeper hiding inside that sentence.
The original Greek reads:
“πρὸ πάντων τὴν εἰς ἑαυτοὺς ἀγάπην ἐκτενῆ ἔχοντες, ὅτι ἀγάπη καλύπτει πλῆθος ἁμαρτιῶν.”
Pro pantōn tēn eis heautous agapēn ektenē echontes, hoti agapē kalyptei plēthos hamartiōn.
The heart of Peter’s command is that believers are to maintain an agapēn ektenē toward one another—an earnest, fervent, intense love.
That word ektenē matters.
Peter is not describing sentimental Christianity.
He is not talking about smiling at somebody on Sunday while quietly resenting them by Monday.
He is describing love that keeps reaching.
Love that remains engaged when relationships become uncomfortable.
Love that does not disappear the moment loving somebody becomes expensive.
And perhaps nobody understood the cost of receiving that kind of love better than Peter.
Because before Peter became the apostle telling Christians that love covers a multitude of sins...
Peter became the disciple whose own failure had to be covered by extraordinary grace.
He had promised Jesus loyalty.
Even if everybody else abandoned Him, Peter insisted that he would remain.
He was confident.
Passionate.
Certain.
Then came the courtyard.
A servant girl recognized him.
“You also were with Jesus.”
And Peter denied it.
Another accusation came.
Another denial.
Then another.
And finally Peter began calling down curses and swearing that he did not know the Man he had once called the Christ.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke records one of the most devastating details in the entire Passion narrative:
“The Lord turned and looked at Peter.” — Luke 22:61
Imagine that moment.
Jesus is being abused.
Rejected.
Dragged toward crucifixion.
And somewhere nearby stands one of His closest friends pretending he has never known Him.
Their eyes meet.
Peter remembers.
And he goes outside and weeps bitterly.
Some of you understand that kind of crying.
The crying that comes when nobody has to expose you anymore because your own conscience already has.
The crying that comes when you realize the person you thought you were and the person you just proved yourself capable of being are not the same person.
Maybe your courtyard looked different.
Maybe nobody heard a rooster.
Maybe yours happened behind a locked bedroom door.
Inside a marriage.
On a phone screen.
In a hotel room.
Inside an addiction nobody knows about.
During an argument when words came out that you can never put back into your mouth.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe somebody betrayed you.
Maybe you promised God, “Never again,” and then found yourself kneeling beside the ruins of the same promise.
Maybe your deepest wound is not what somebody did to you.
Maybe it is what you did.
And maybe somewhere beneath your worship songs, Bible verses, Christian posts, Sunday clothes, ministry responsibilities, and carefully constructed smile lives one terrifying question:
Would Jesus still want me if everyone knew?
Peter knew that question.
And Jesus answered it.
Not by pretending Peter never sinned.
Not by calling betrayal harmless.
Not by redefining darkness as light.
Jesus went to the cross.
This distinction matters enormously when Peter later says that “love covers a multitude of sins.”
Peter is not saying our love pays for sin.
Only Christ can do that.
Peter did not die for Peter’s sins.
Jesus did.
You cannot love yourself into justification.
Your spouse cannot forgive you into reconciliation with God.
A church cannot overlook enough mistakes to wash a guilty conscience clean before a holy God.
The blood of Jesus Christ does what human affection never could.
At the cross, Jesus bears sin.
Jesus satisfies justice.
Jesus becomes the once-for-all sacrifice.
Jesus purchases redemption.
Jesus reconciles sinners to God.
Jesus saves.
So when Peter says love “covers” sins, he is not replacing the cross.
He is showing us what people transformed by the cross begin to look like.
And Peter appears to be drawing from an ancient proverb.
Proverbs 10:12 says:
“Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all offenses.”
The Hebrew contains this striking contrast:
“שִׂנְאָה תְּעוֹרֵר מְדָנִים וְעַל כָּל־פְּשָׁעִים תְּכַסֶּה אַהֲבָה”
Sin'ah te'orer medanim, ve'al kol-pesha'im tekhasseh ahavah.
Hatred stirs up conflicts.
Love covers offenses.
Notice the contrast.
Hatred uncovers things because hatred wants ammunition.
Love covers because love does not delight in using another person’s weakness as a weapon.
Hatred keeps receipts.
Hatred replays conversations.
Hatred collects evidence.
Hatred tells the story again, slightly worse each time.
Hatred wants an audience.
Hatred whispers, “Do you know what they did?”
Love asks a completely different question:
“How can redemption win here?”
That does not mean biblical love hides abuse.
It does not mean concealing crimes.
It does not mean protecting predators.
It does not mean refusing accountability.
It does not mean pretending unrepentant evil is acceptable.
It does not mean remaining indefinitely in dangerous circumstances.
And it certainly does not mean calling sin righteousness.
The same New Testament that commands fervent love also commands truth, repentance, correction, justice, wisdom, church discipline, and protection of the vulnerable.
Biblical love does not cooperate with darkness.
But biblical love also refuses to turn another person’s ordinary failures, repented sins, weaknesses, awkwardness, and offenses into entertainment.
There is a difference between exposing darkness so healing can begin and exposing a person because humiliation feels satisfying.
There is a difference between accountability and revenge.
There is a difference between telling the truth and enjoying someone’s downfall.
There is a difference between refusing to enable sin and refusing to forgive a repentant sinner.
And sometimes the most revealing question is not:
“Did they sin?”
They may have.
The more revealing question is:
“What does my heart want to happen to them now?”
That question hurts.
Because sometimes we say we want justice when what we secretly want is humiliation.
Sometimes we say we are warning people when we are actually enjoying the attention their failure gives us.
Sometimes we call it discernment when bitterness has simply learned Christian vocabulary.
Sometimes we keep telling a forgiven story because we enjoy being the innocent character in it.
Peter will not let us stay there.
“Above all... love.”
Why above all?
Look at the surrounding passage.
Peter says the end of all things is near.
Be sober-minded.
Pray.
Love one another earnestly.
Show hospitality without grumbling.
Use your gifts to serve one another.
Speak as one entrusted with God’s words.
Serve with strength God supplies.
And then Peter reveals where all of this is supposed to lead:
“So that in everything God may be glorified through Jesus Christ.”
There it is.
The destination is the glory of God through Jesus Christ.
Not our reputation.
Not our platform.
Not our ability to win arguments.
Not our ability to appear spiritually superior.
Jesus.
Peter is describing a community living so close to eternity that petty hatred begins to look ridiculous.
The end is near...
so pray.
The end is near...
so love.
The end is near...
so open your home.
The end is near...
so serve.
The end is near...
so stop wasting your remaining days feeding grudges that Jesus died to teach you how to surrender.
And suddenly Peter’s words become painfully personal.
Because there is probably somebody whose name changes your heartbeat.
Someone you avoid.
Someone whose apology never seemed sufficient.
Someone you have forgiven with your mouth but continue prosecuting inside your imagination.
Or perhaps you are on the other side.
Perhaps you are the one hoping somebody will believe that Jesus can change you.
Perhaps people still introduce you through your worst chapter.
The addict.
The adulterer.
The liar.
The failure.
The divorced one.
The prodigal.
The hypocrite.
The one who ruined everything.
People have a frightening ability to freeze someone inside the worst thing they ever did.
Jesus does not.
Ask Peter.
After the resurrection, Jesus meets him again.
Not in a courtroom.
Beside a charcoal fire.
There is something beautiful about that detail.
John’s Gospel uses the word for charcoal fire when Peter denies Jesus and again when the risen Christ meets His disciples by the sea.
Peter once stood near a fire denying that he knew Jesus.
Now he stands near another fire looking into the face of the Jesus he denied.
You can almost feel the memory hanging in the smoke.
Jesus asks:
“Simon, son of John, do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
Three denials.
Three questions.
But Jesus is not torturing Peter.
He is restoring him.
And after Peter answers, Jesus keeps saying, in essence:
Feed My sheep.
Think about that.
Jesus entrusted wounded people to a man who had failed Him.
Peter’s scandal did not become the final sentence of Peter’s story.
Grace wrote another chapter.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin does not matter.
Sin matters so much that the Son of God went to a cross.
But grace is so astonishing that the cross can transform sinners instead of merely identifying them.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin was never serious.”
The Gospel says, “Your sin was so serious Christ died—and His grace is so powerful that His death and resurrection can make you new.”
This is why Christian love can cover offenses.
Because Christians live beneath a greater covering.
We have received mercy we did not earn.
We have been forgiven debts we could never repay.
We stand before God not displaying our spotless record but trusting the spotless righteousness of Christ.
How strange, then, when forgiven people become addicted to exposing everyone else.
How strange when recipients of mercy become stingy with mercy.
How strange when people whose eternal hope rests upon grace begin treating another believer as though one failure has permanently disqualified them from ever becoming anything else.
Peter knew better.
He had lived it.
He knew what it meant for Jesus to know the entire truth about him and still call him.
And maybe that is the part somebody reading this needs tonight.
Jesus knows.
Not the edited version.
Not the testimony version where everything ugly has already been cleaned up enough for church.
He knows what actually happened.
He knows what you clicked.
He knows what you said.
He knows who you hurt.
He knows what you crave.
He knows what you hide.
He knows the thought that frightened even you.
He knows the promise you broke.
He knows the night you wish could disappear from history.
And still the Gospel invitation stands:
Repent.
Come home.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His mercy is greater.
Repentance is not God demanding that you repair yourself before approaching Him.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can rescue you from it.
There is forgiveness in Jesus.
There is cleansing in Jesus.
There is restoration in Jesus.
There is a new identity in Jesus.
There is no scandal so impressive that it can intimidate the blood of Christ.
But grace does not merely comfort the guilty.
Grace changes how the forgiven treat other guilty people.
So perhaps Peter’s words need to enter your marriage tonight.
Love deeply.
Perhaps they need to enter your church.
Love deeply.
Perhaps they need to enter a friendship damaged by misunderstanding.
Love deeply.
Perhaps they need to enter the comment section before you type something designed to embarrass another human being.
Love deeply.
Perhaps they need to enter the family group chat.
Love deeply.
Perhaps they need to enter the room where two believers have been keeping score for ten years.
Love deeply.
Not foolishly.
Not dishonestly.
Not without boundaries where boundaries are necessary.
Not without truth.
But deeply.
Because love is not pretending there was no wound.
Love is refusing to worship the wound.
Love does not always erase consequences.
It refuses to make revenge its god.
Love can confront.
Love can say, “That was wrong.”
Love can require repentance.
Love can establish boundaries.
Love can protect the vulnerable.
Love can weep.
Love can walk through a long process of rebuilding trust.
But love refuses to become hatred wearing a Bible verse.
And this is where Peter’s words stop being a beautiful quotation and become a cross-shaped way of life.
Who are you still trying to punish?
Whose worst moment have you turned into their permanent identity?
Whose failure secretly makes you feel better about yourself?
And what are you still hiding because you are terrified that grace might be available for everyone except you?
Bring it to Jesus.
No performance.
No religious camouflage.
No hiding.
If this exposed something you have buried, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But you can take one honest step.
Comment, “Jesus, teach me to love deeply.”
If what you really need is prayer, comment, “pray for me.”
If you have been carrying shame from a chapter Christ is redeeming, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And if you are exhausted from pretending everything is fine, perhaps your words are simply:
“No more hiding.”
There may be someone reading the comments who thought they were the only one fighting that battle.
Your honesty may remind them that the Church is not a museum for people who never needed mercy.
It is a people gathered around a crucified and risen Savior.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this, do more than quietly agree with these words.
Send this to them.
Send it to the believer who is struggling to forgive.
Send it to the prodigal who thinks church doors are permanently closed.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is nothing more than religious people pretending to be better than everybody else.
Let them see what Christianity actually announces:
We are not saved because we were better.
We are saved because Jesus is merciful.
Because eventually somebody will hurt you.
Eventually you will disappoint somebody.
Eventually you may need to remember that Peter did not say love covers sins because sin is insignificant.
He said it because redeemed communities cannot survive if every failure becomes ammunition.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin honestly, understand grace more deeply, and keep your eyes fixed on Jesus, stay close.
Live them.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Repent where the Spirit exposes sin.
Seek reconciliation where reconciliation is possible.
Speak truth without cruelty.
Set wise boundaries without surrendering your heart to hatred.
Protect the vulnerable.
Restore the repentant.
Carry one another’s burdens.
Stop turning people’s scars into their names.
And remember the fisherman who once swore that he never knew Jesus.
That same man became an apostle who strengthened the Church.
The mouth that denied Christ eventually preached Christ.
The man who collapsed under fear eventually suffered for the name he once denied.
Grace did not rewrite Peter’s past by pretending it never happened.
Grace rewrote what his past was allowed to mean.
And Jesus is still doing that.
Maybe even now.
Maybe in you.
Maybe in the person you have almost given up on.
Maybe in the person staring back at you from the mirror.
Because when Jesus gets the final word, your worst chapter does not get to name the whole book.
Somewhere between the fire where Peter denied Jesus and the fire where Jesus restored him, scandal lost the right to write the ending.
